scenes.title: The economic cost of the war
scenes.visual: The host appears beside war footage, headlines and economic graphics.

paragraphs.text: The opening asks what years of fighting have done to Russia's and Ukraine's economies. Military spending and forces have grown while the front has become a **war of attrition**.
The host proposes to examine GDP, budgets, debt, military spending, trade and interest rates, while warning that **headline figures can hide the human consequences**.
Translated captions (automated, in time order):

Friends, Russia has been at war with Ukraine for more than four years. You said their current economy? What exactly is going on that we may be in the news headlines recently? I see less and less relevant information, but in fact The war continues to expand in scope and scope Both sides continue to increase their military expenditures and the number of troops on the front line. It just gradually fell into a tug-of-war of attrition. Then I'm curious. You said that apart from the situation on the battlefield itself, What kind of impact has it had on the Russian and Ukrainian economies? The economic structures of both sides What kind of great changes have taken place? It’s almost exhausted. I have gradually found some new ways. Let me tell you.

I have done an in-depth study of GDP, inflation, debt and military spending on both sides. A lot of data such as trade interest rates were also combined with some research report analysis to understand it. These data are objective but also deceptive. Let’s take a look today. What will war do to a country's economy?

scenes.title: 2022: Russia absorbs the first shock
scenes.visual: Maps, sanctions headlines and graphics about the ruble, rates and energy prices appear.

paragraphs.text: The host reviews the 2022 invasion and sanctions: Ukrainian infrastructure was damaged, millions were displaced, and Western countries froze **roughly $300 billion of Russian reserves**. Energy and food markets were disrupted.

Russia faced a falling ruble and capital flight. The video says its central bank raised rates **from 9.5% to 20%** and imposed capital controls, while oil sales to China and India and high prices supported revenue. The host calls this **a shock Russia endured without an economic collapse**.
Translated captions (automated, in time order):

First of all, let’s go through the big picture in chronological order. What happened on both sides of the overall macroeconomic performance? Later, we will analyze it in depth by detailed items. On February 24, 2022, the Russo-Ukrainian war broke out and Russia’s original blitzkrieg The plan to capture Kiev within a few days failed Later, it was adjusted to a deep advance in Donbass. Ukraine lost ground at first but withstood the huge initial pressure in the autumn. Launched the Kharkov and Kherson counterattacks and Russia was forced to shrink its front Ukraine has indeed suffered widespread infrastructure destruction. Tens of millions of people are displaced and the West faces Russia

Implemented unprecedented financial and trade sanctions to kick it out of the Swift system Freezes its $300 billion in foreign exchange reserves Do you think Russia is a major energy producer, but Ukraine is a major food producer? Therefore, the war directly led to the global plunge in 2022 Energy crisis and food crisis are good This is the general background of the first stage. So how is the Russian economy this year? I can sum it up in one word: In fact, let’s withdraw these foreign capital from financial controls. The most serious impact it will have in the short term is the collapse of the ruble But let me tell you, there is a very powerful person in Russia, the governor of its central bank.

Called Sister Nabiullin, she is a high-level decision-maker in Russia. It can be said that he has a lot of say and is known as "Putin's firefighter" Putin's Firefighter, according to Bloomberg She submitted her resignation to Putin twice in 2022 and 2024 I wanted to resign but was rejected by Putin. What’s the specific reason? It’s not very clear to the outside world, but it’s certain that in Russia It will be difficult to find a replacement for her At that time, facing the plummeting ruble in 2022, Sister Na made a prompt decision. Directly violently raise the interest rate from 9.5% to 20% Coupled with policies such as compulsory foreign exchange settlement and capital controls, this has stabilized the ruble's exchange rate.

At the same time, China and India have taken on a large part of the oil demand that Europe has withdrawn from. Coupled with the rising oil prices, Russia has benefited from energy dividends. This oil revenue has hit a record high, helping the ruble to rebound further and even Bouncing to a level more valuable than before the war, Russia’s economy in 2022 Russia's economy actually shrank by 1.4% this year is far better than Western predictions

scenes.title: 2022: Ukraine's output collapses
scenes.visual: A graphic highlights a roughly 28.8% GDP contraction alongside refugees and damaged cities.

paragraphs.text: The video reports **a 28.8% fall in Ukraine's GDP in 2022**, **close to a third of annual output**. Lost territory, damaged infrastructure and **roughly eight million people leaving the country** further reduced productive capacity.
The host notes that Ukraine entered the full-scale war with a fragile economy and income per person below Russia's. External support kept it functioning but could not offset the scale of destruction.
Translated captions (automated, in time order):

What about Ukraine? Don’t look at it on the battlefield. Economically, we just said that Russia is “holding it together and not collapsing.” Ukraine is really in ruins. Let’s not talk about anything else and let’s look at GDP data: Ukraine’s GDP growth rate in 2022 It's -28.8%, and that doesn't even include GDP during the war. It may be artificially high. In short, it is 1/3 of the economic output value within a year. Many of them disappeared and were just spent on the war. and repairing damage caused by war and territorial loss The infrastructure for population flight has been largely destroyed. There are approximately 8 million refugees fleeing the country. In fact, it accounts for almost 1/5 of its population.

The Ukrainian economy was already in bad shape before the war started. Don’t think so. Ukraine has joined the EU and is not far from Germany, so the economy must be good. Even if it's not as good as Germany, then it should be similar to Italy. Hey, that's not the case at all. We always joke about it. Italy is a member of the European Pig Five and its economy is in a mess It also depends on who you are comparing with. Just look at GDP per capita. Russia is less than half the size of Italy and Ukraine is Less than half of Russia In fact, since the conflict in Donbass in 2014 Ukraine's economy has already begun to collapse, so some people say

The Russo-Ukrainian war had already begun at that time If we compare Ukraine to a person, then it was actually before the war started There are already a lot of major and minor ailments, which belongs to that sub-health state. But people in Russia secretly practiced at home for a long time and learned various fighting skills. This guy came up and kicked the door. Ukraine must have been beaten badly. Thanks to the large amount of aid from other countries, it was able to hold on and not go into shock. But overall these aids are only a drop in the bucket for Ukraine's economy. In fact, Ukraine basically had no economy at that time.

scenes.title: 2023–24: War production and inflation
scenes.visual: The host is intercut with battlefield, factory and inflation graphics.

paragraphs.text: As the fighting becomes prolonged, the host calls Russia's military production an **economic stimulant**. The video reports **GDP growth above 4% in both years**, but says private activity was crowded out. Inflation rose **from below 3% in mid-2023 to almost 10% by late 2024**, and the **central-bank rate reached 21%**.

Ukraine recovered from a low base, with reported growth of **5.5% in 2023 and 3.2% in 2024**. Its war spending and public finances depended heavily on US and European assistance. Both economies faced renewed price pressure.
Translated captions (automated, in time order):

Russia makes slow territorial gains in eastern Ukraine But at the same time, it also paid a high price because the cost of advancing the front was too high. Both sides are gradually moving into using human artillery drones Go to the stage of grinding bit by bit If I were asked to sum up the Russian economy in the past two years in one word, I would use military stimulants That is to say, the economy of the entire country They are all leaning towards a military-industrial complex. It can be said that the country has been injected with chicken blood. In fact, in the past two years, the Russian economy has It also has another theme, which is the shift to eastern energy exports.

Further tilt towards Asia through the shadow fleet, but as for the military industry, I personally think that It has a greater impact on Russia’s overall economy, so it is a key word in this stage. On steroids, Russia’s GDP growth has exceeded 4% in the past two years. Its military expenditure has increased significantly. The military industry has exploded and is extremely short of manpower. The private sector shrinks further The whole country is becoming more and more like a war machine What is accompanied by this is that inflation in the entire country begins to rise. Already showing signs of overheating, less than 3% by mid-2023 But by the end of 2024, it has climbed to nearly 10%, forcing the Russian Central Bank to That firefighter, Sister Na, went out again

Now the interest rate has been directly raised to 21%. At the same time, due to the drop in oil prices, Oil revenues are also declining, forcing Russia to tap into its sovereign funds To fill this liquidity, we will talk about it in detail later. As for the economy in Ukraine, it can be summed up in one word: slow recovery. GDP growth rate in 2023 is 5.5% and 3.2% in 2024 It is also far lower than market expectations. At the same time, it still has a huge war burden. So it’s the real life-saver for the economy. In fact, it is a huge amount of external blood transfusion The United States and the European Union provide Ukraine with $60 billion to $80 billion in funding each year This is more than all the revenue of the Ukrainian government combined

At the same time, what will happen if Ukraine's internal economy has suffered a serious blow? In case of inflation, if supply is insufficient, prices will rise. So its inflation has come down from the high point at the beginning of the war. The results have climbed again in 24 years. You see two countries. have fallen into inflation, so inflation can be said to be War is a chronic disease that will always accompany it.

scenes.title: 2025–26: Aid and fiscal limits
scenes.visual: US and European policy footage alternates with growth and debt charts.

paragraphs.text: The video treats changes in external support as the central development: US aid was interrupted, Ukraine reached a minerals agreement with the US, and Europe proposed a much larger loan package. The host argues that **financing has become decisive**.

Russia's earlier military stimulus comes with weaker private investment and consumption; the video puts its 2025 growth near 1%. **Ukraine's public debt exceeds 100% of GDP** and reported **2025 growth is around 1.8%**, leaving output below its prewar level.

scenes.title: People are the scarcest resource
scenes.visual: Casualty estimates, refugee footage and population charts appear.

paragraphs.text: The host stresses that **casualty counts are highly uncertain**: estimates from the belligerents and third parties vary widely, so no single figure should be treated as exact. The larger economic shock may be displacement.

The video estimates that **about 16 million Ukrainians have left their homes**, **roughly 40% of the prewar population**, with six to eight million leaving the country at some point. Losing workers affects production, tax receipts and rebuilding. Ukraine can receive money and equipment from abroad, but **replacing people is much harder**.
Translated captions (automated, in time order):

Okay, we just took a very general look at it. The general outline of the economies on both sides will become more interesting next. Let’s take a closer look at the impact of the war on both sides. The first is the most important, the lowest, and the bottom. Sometimes we analyze economic issues. One point that may be overlooked is that I don’t know about you. Anyway, when it comes to war, my first feeling is that I want to know more about it. The casualties on both sides made me realize the scale of the entire war. resources money manpower but russia The population is 3.6 times that of Ukraine and the GDP is more than 10 times that of Ukraine. What about Ukraine? If you talk about resources, money and weapons? scenes.title: Russia's labor shortage
scenes.visual: Charts show unemployment, labor compensation and demand for workers.

paragraphs.text: Russia has not seen displacement on Ukraine's scale, but its armed forces, defense factories and civilian employers compete for the same people. The host explains that **extremely low unemployment can signal a labor shortage** and an overheated economy.

The video says labor compensation rose **from about 41% of GDP before the war to roughly 50.2% in the first half of 2025**. Higher wages help some workers but raise business costs, reinforce inflation and squeeze civilian production.
Translated captions (automated, in time order):

On the other hand, things are different here in Russia. There is also a shortage of people. But because there is no large-scale population fleeing large-scale population movements So it’s just a scarcity at the labor level. Especially after the military stimulants we just mentioned were introduced The labor force is extremely scarce, as we mentioned in the previous summary. Russia experienced economic overheating in 2024. On the one hand, it was high inflation. On the other hand, Russia has also experienced A very major problem facing the economy is the extremely low unemployment rate You have to know that the unemployment rate does not mean that the lower the better, everyone has a job. If the unemployment rate is 0%, it is perfect. In fact, it is a healthy economy.

There will always be some people who want to resign and find a job. Everyone is in a working state. To put it professionally, there will be a natural rate of unemployment This number is about 4% to 6%, which is relatively healthy if the unemployment rate Sustainably lower than the natural rate of unemployment It shows that the entire economy is a bit deformed due to excessive shortage of people. This is actually a manifestation of economic overheating. Just look at this. This is the unemployment rate in Russia since 2022, right? I don’t need to say anything more. Its central bank governor, Sister Na, has publicly stated many times that there is a labor shortage. The shortage of people is the main reason why Russia’s current economy is overheating.

So companies have to pay higher wages to grab people. Even government departments and state-owned enterprises are no exception Russia’s overall labor remuneration as a share of GDP from 41% before the war Rising to 50.2% in the first half of 2025 Like a female textile worker, machine tool worker, delivery worker, truck driver In recent years, the national average salary has doubled that of Russian contract soldiers. Although this treaty does not clearly state how to transport people, after this At least 10,000 North Korean combat troops were dispatched and 50,000 to 100,000 laborers were dispatched. So what is the strategic partnership method? The first thing is to send people to Russia.

scenes.title: Budgets, frozen assets and aid
scenes.visual: EU meetings, reserve and gold charts, and aid and budget graphics appear.

paragraphs.text: The video says Russian military spending rose **from about 3.7% of GDP in 2021 to about 7.5% in 2025**. A large share of the **roughly $300 billion in frozen Russian reserves** is held in Europe. Governments disagree over confiscating principal, so European support has relied more on profits or loans backed by future income from those assets.

The host distinguishes reserves, which buffer shocks, from a sovereign wealth fund intended for longer-term investment. Russia has drawn on the fund; higher gold prices support its book value, but **liquid resources remain strained**.

Ukraine devotes a much larger share of its output to war and depends on Western aid. The video reports roughly €350 billion in direct support by early 2026, about 33% from the US and 59% from Europe. It argues that IMF loans, though smaller and conditional, also unlock confidence and financing from other donors.

The Russian government Its financial situation was actually not optimistic in the first year of the war. Because the government revenue was particularly high because it reaped the dividends of the energy crisis, that year The government fiscal deficit accounts for only 1.2% of GDP, but what happens next? The foreign exchange government on all platforms at the Russian national level is also good The central bank, for example, mainly has these two piles of foreign exchange reserves. As for this sovereign fund, normally some countries are very, very wealthy. I was thinking about taking some money from the foreign exchange reserves to invest in something. For investment in 10 or 20 years In order to support ourselves in the future and raise children, we have made two videos before I talked about the top ten sovereign funds in the world. If you are interested, you can go back and take a look.

Then you think of it, Russia is also an energy powerhouse and its sovereign fund is not small. Before the war begins in 2021, its foreign exchange reserves will be approximately US$600 billion. scenes.title: Similar inflation, different causes
